planting.note: Direct-sow in late summer to early fall so seedlings form overwintering rosettes before bolting to bloom the following spring; a light spring sowing is possible in mild climates but delays flowering to the second year.

directions: This selection carries irregular cream-to-white splashes and margins on its coarse heart-shaped leaves, giving winter and early-spring rosettes garden interest well before the purple four-petaled flowers open in the second spring. Site it where the patterned foliage can be appreciated at the front of a part-shade border or woodland edge, since variegation shows best with some protection from the hottest midday sun. The same translucent silvery seedpods prized on the plain species form here, and because variegated plants self-seed with variable leaf pattern, periodically rogue out any all-green seedlings to keep the planting consistently patterned. Give moist, humusy, well-drained soil for the strongest two-tone leaf color.

planting.note: Direct-sow in late summer to early fall for overwintering rosettes and spring-of-second-year bloom; sow fresh seed, since older honesty seed loses vigor quickly in storage.

directions: A pure white-flowered selection of common honesty, lacking the purple pigment of the species and giving a cleaner, brighter look through its spring flowering spikes in a part-shade cottage border or woodland-edge planting. Flowers are followed by the same flat, papery, silver-dollar seedpods that dry to translucency and are cut for everlasting arrangements. Because honesty cross-pollinates freely, grow 'Alba' away from purple-flowered plants if you want seed-grown offspring to stay true white, and expect some reversion to purple in mixed colonies over successive self-sown generations. Otherwise culture matches the species: moist, fertile, well-drained soil and benign neglect once established.

planting.note: Direct-sow or transplant young plants in late summer to early fall; the dark foliage color develops most strongly on seedlings grown on in cooler conditions rather than summer heat.

directions: Marketed under the trade name Corfu Beauty, this selection carries deep purple-flushed foliage and stems that set off its clusters of purple honesty flowers far more dramatically than the plain green-leaved species. The dark coloring is most intense on young rosette leaves through winter and fades somewhat as summer heat arrives, so part shade and cool, moist soil help preserve the strongest tone into the flowering season. As with other honesty selections, the large flat seedpods ripen to papery silver discs for drying, and self-sown seedlings may show variable leaf darkness since the trait segregates in open-pollinated offspring. Use it as a foliage accent at a border edge where the purple leaves can be seen against lighter companions.

planting.note: Direct-sow in late summer to early fall for overwintering rosettes and bloom the following spring, in the dappled light of a woodland-edge or shrub border planting.

directions: A deep violet-purple-flowered selection of honesty tracing to the historic Munstead Wood garden, giving noticeably richer, more saturated flower color than the lavender-purple of the common wild form. Its spring flower spikes attract early bees and butterflies in a part-shade cottage or woodland-edge planting, and the flat round seedpods that follow dry to the same prized silvery, papery discs used in dried arrangements. Because honesty readily self-seeds and crosses with other color forms nearby, isolate it from paler-flowered honesty if you want to maintain the deep purple strain from saved seed. Otherwise it is carefree in any moist, well-drained garden soil.
sources: Jekka's Herb Farm / heritage seed catalogs

planting.note: Direct-sow in late summer to early fall; dark-leaved honesty selections like this one are often started a touch earlier than the species so rosettes size up before the first hard frost.

directions: This honesty selection, associated with the English garden designer whose name it carries, pairs white spring flowers with foliage that carries a distinct purple-bronze flush, a combination prized by UK specialist perennial nurseries for cottage-garden and woodland-edge plantings. The pairing of pale flowers against dark leaves reads more strongly than either trait alone and makes a useful color echo near purple-leaved shrubs or dark hellebores. Flowering is followed by the same flat, silvery seedpods typical of the species, valued fresh on the plant and cut for drying. Give it the same moist, humus-rich, part-shaded site as other honesty forms, and expect self-sown seedlings to vary in leaf darkness since the trait is not fixed in open-pollinated populations.

planting.note: Sow in late summer for overwintering rosettes that bloom the following year, in dappled woodland-edge shade; this peloric form breeds somewhat true from isolated seed but a minority of seedlings revert to the normal spire form.

directions: An old curiosity among foxgloves, this heirloom peloric (hose-in-hose) form replaces the normal terminal bell with a second, upward-facing bell nested inside the first at the top of the spike, a teratological trait that has fascinated gardeners and botanists for generations. Below that odd terminal flower, the spike carries the typical pendent, spotted-throat bells of common foxglove on tall stems well suited to the back of a part-shade woodland border. Because the trait segregates in seedlings, rogue out any plants that fail to show the doubled terminal bell if you want to keep a strain selected for the feature, and otherwise grow it exactly as you would any purpurea foxglove, in moist, humus-rich soil with light shade from afternoon sun.
